content: Didanosine, whether used alone or in combination with other medications, has the potential to cause severe liver and pancreatic damage, as well as a condition known as lactic acidosis. Inform your doctor if you currently consume or have previously consumed large amounts of alcohol, if you use or have used illicit drugs, or if you have a history of Crohn's disease, cystic fibrosis, diabetes, high cholesterol, or liver or pancreatic disease. Additionally, notify your doctor and pharmacist if you are taking stavudine (Zerit), particularly if you are pregnant. It is crucial to inform your healthcare provider and pharmacist if you are currently taking or have taken any of the following medications: acetaminophen (Tylenol, others); allopurinol (Zyloprim); amiodarone (Cordarone, Pacerone); azathioprine (Imuran); statins (cholesterol-lowering medications); dantrolene (Dantrium); furosemide (Lasix); hormone replacement therapy; iron supplements; isoniazid (INH, Nydrazid); ketoconazole (Nizoral); HIV or AIDS medications; 6-mercaptopurine (Purinethol); methotrexate (Rheumatrex); methyldopa (Aldoril); niacin (nicotinic acid); oral contraceptives; oral steroids such as dexamethasone (Decadron, Dexone), methylprednisolone (Medrol), and prednisone (Deltasone); pentamidine (Nebupent, Pentam); piroxicam (Feldene); pyrazinamide (Rifater); ribavirin (Rebetron); rifampin (Rifadin, Rimactane); salicylate pain relievers such as aspirin, choline magnesium trisalicylate (Trisalate), choline salicylate (Arthropan), diflunisal (Dolobid), magnesium salicylate (Doan's, others), and salsalate (Argesic, Disalcid, Salgesic); sulfonamide antibiotics such as sulfadiazine, sulfamethizole (Urobiotic), sulfasalazine (Azulfidine), and sulfisoxazole (Eryzole, Gantrisin, Pediazole); sulindac (Clinoril); valproic acid (Depakene, Depakote); or products containing kava. If you experience symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, abdominal pain or swelling, severe back pain, extreme fatigue, weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness, rapid heartbeat, sudden onset of a slow or irregular heartbeat, deep or rapid breathing, shortness of breath, dark yellow or brown urine, unusual bleeding or bruising, yellowing of the skin or eyes, feeling cold, fever, or flu-like symptoms, contact your doctor immediately. Discuss with your doctor the safe use of alcohol while taking didanosine, as alcohol consumption can heighten the risk of severe side effects. Didanosine is prescribed in combination with other medications to treat HIV infection in patients with or without AIDS. It belongs to a class of drugs called nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and works by slowing the spread of HIV in the body. However, it does not cure HIV, prevent HIV-related illnesses, or stop the transmission of HIV to others. Didanosine is available in various forms, including extended-release capsules, chewable tablets, powder for oral solution, and liquid solution. It is typically taken once or twice daily on an empty stomach, either 30 minutes before or 2 hours after eating. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully and take the medication exactly as directed. Do not alter the dosage or frequency without consulting your doctor. For extended-release capsules, swallow them whole without splitting, chewing, crushing, or opening them. Chewable tablets should be chewed thoroughly or dissolved in at least 1 ounce of water before swallowing. You may add 1 ounce of clear apple juice for flavor if needed, but avoid using other juices. Powder should be mixed with 4 ounces of water immediately before consumption and stirred until fully dissolved. Do not mix the powder with fruit juice or other liquids. Continue taking didanosine even if you feel well, as it controls but does not cure HIV infection. Do not stop taking the medication without consulting your doctor, as missed doses or discontinuation can make your condition harder to treat. Didanosine may also be used in combination with other medications to prevent HIV infection in healthcare workers or individuals accidentally exposed to the virus. Discuss the potential risks of this use with your doctor. Before starting didanosine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to didanosine, aspartame, antacids, or any other substances. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, and supplements you are taking, as some may interact with didanosine. Certain medications must be taken several hours before or after didanosine; consult your doctor for specific timing instructions. Inform your doctor if you are on a low-salt diet or have a history of eye disease, muscle problems, gout, peripheral neuropathy, radiation therapy, phenylketonuria (PKU), or heart or kidney disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. Breastfeeding is not recommended for individuals with HIV or those taking didanosine. Be aware that didanosine may cause serious side effects that require immediate treatment. Children taking didanosine may not be able to communicate these side effects, so caregivers should learn to recognize them. Additionally, didanosine may cause changes in body fat distribution, such as increased fat in the breasts or upper back. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Minor side effects of didanosine include diarrhea, headache, and muscle pain. Severe side effects, though uncommon, require immediate medical attention and include hives, rash, itching, difficulty breathing or swallowing, numbness or pain in the hands or feet, blurred vision, difficulty distinguishing colors, and chills. Report any unusual symptoms to your doctor. Store didanosine capsules, tablets, and powder in their original containers at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Liquid solutions should be refrigerated and discarded after 30 days. Mixtures of tablets and apple juice should be used within 1 hour, and mixtures of powder and water within 4 hours. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Symptoms of overdose may include diarrhea, numbness or pain in the hands or feet, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, abdominal pain or swelling, severe back pain, extreme fatigue, weakness, dizziness, rapid or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, dark urine, unusual bleeding or bruising, yellowing of the skin or eyes, feeling cold, fever, or flu-like symptoms. Do not share this medication with others. If you spill didanosine powder or liquid, clean the area with soap and water, avoiding the creation of airborne dust. Wash your hands and cleaning materials thoroughly afterward.
